SOHO devices typically include an access point for wireless devices.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 26

stem: Which of the following is a correct definition of a collision domain?
options: A group of local area networks (LANs) connected by routers, thus enabling any node to transmit to any other node
A group of computers connected so that a broadcast transmission by any one device reaches all of the other devices
A group of devices connected by cable segments that are longer than the maximum length stated in the physical layer specification
A group of devices connected so that when two devices transmit at exactly the same time, a data collision occurs
explanation: A collision domain is a LAN with a shared network medium, so that two devices transmitting at the same time generate a signal quality error, also known as a collision. Ethernet LANs connected by hubs create a shared medium, whereas switched networks create a separate collision domain for each connected node. Routers create separate collision domains. A group of computers able to receive broadcasts is the definition of a broadcast domain, not a collision domain. Overlong cables can precipitate collisions but do not define a collision domain.
whyWrong: LANs connected by routers form an internetwork, not a collision domain.
A group that receives each other’s broadcasts is a broadcast domain.
Overlong cables can cause collisions but do not define a collision domain.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 28

stem: A VPN headend is an advanced type of which of the following devices?
explanation: A virtual private network (VPN) headend is a type of router that enables multiple client systems to access a network from remote locations. Because the device provides an interface between networks, it is considered to be a type of router, not a switch, a gateway, or a bridge.
whyWrong: A switch forwards frames inside one network by MAC address and does not connect remote clients across networks.
A gateway is a general term for a device that translates between different protocols or systems, not the device type a VPN headend is built on.
A bridge joins segments of the same network at the Data link layer and does not route traffic between networks.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 29

stem: An enterprise network has been designed with individual departmental switches because, in most cases, the devices in a specific department exchange network traffic with other devices in the same department. Each of the departmental switches is also connected to a host switch, which enables devices to communicate with other departments. Which of the following terms describes this switching architecture?
explanation: Distributed switching describes a hierarchical switching architecture in which remote switches (departmental switches in this case) handle most of the network traffic, with a host switch used only for traffic between the remote locations. Port forwarding is a routing method that redirects traffic intended for one IP address and port number to another. Traffic shaping is a series of techniques that optimizes the allocation of network bandwidth. Neighbor discovery is an IPv6 technique used to find addresses of devices and services on the local network. Flow control is a technique for regulating a system's transmission speed.
whyWrong: Port forwarding redirects traffic sent to one IP address and port to another, which is not a switching architecture.
Traffic shaping controls how bandwidth is allocated to traffic, not how switches are arranged.
Neighbor discovery is an IPv6 method for finding devices on the local link, not a switching architecture.
Flow control regulates how fast a system transmits, not how switches are arranged.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 41
note: Distributed switching is not named in N10-009; tagged to the three-tier hierarchical model as the closest topic.

stem: Which of the following could be a valid MAC address for a network interface adapter?
explanation: A media access control (MAC) address is a 6-byte hexadecimal value, with the bytes separated by colons, as in 00:1A:6B:31:9A:4E. The value 10.124.25.43 uses decimal numbers and periods, so it is an IPv4 address. FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF has a valid MAC format, but it is reserved as the broadcast address. The value 03:AE:16:3H:5B:11 is not valid, because hexadecimal uses only numerals and the letters A to F. The value fe80::89a5:9e4d:a9d0:9ed7 is too long for a MAC address; it is an IPv6 address.
whyWrong: This value uses decimal numbers separated by periods, so it is an IPv4 address.
This value is reserved as the Ethernet broadcast address and cannot belong to one adapter.
This value contains the letter H, which is not a hexadecimal digit.
This value is far too long for a MAC address and is an IPv6 link-local address.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 43

stem: Which of the following cable types can be used to connect an MDI port on a workstation to an Auto-MDI-X port on an Ethernet switch? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: When connecting an MDI port to an Auto-MDI-X port, it is possible to use either a straight-through or a crossover cable because the Auto-MDI-X port can self-adjust to implement the necessary crossover circuit if it is needed. MDI and Auto-MDI-X ports are used only with twisted-pair cables, so there is no need for coaxial or fiber-optic cables.
whyWrong: MDI and Auto-MDI-X ports are twisted-pair ports, so coaxial cable cannot connect to them.
Single-mode fiber needs fiber ports and transceivers, not MDI or Auto-MDI-X twisted-pair ports.
Multimode fiber needs fiber ports and transceivers, not MDI or Auto-MDI-X twisted-pair ports.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 45
note: MDI/MDI-X and crossover cables are not named in N10-009; tagged to wired media (802.3 standards).

stem: Each of the following Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD) events occurs on an Ethernet network when two stations transmit simultaneously, although not in the order listed. Which of the following events occurs immediately after the collision?
options: The two stations observe a random backoff interval.
The two stations transmit a jam signal.
The two stations listen to see if the channel is idle.
The two stations begin retransmitting their frames.
explanation: Stations on a CSMA/CD network first check the medium to see if it is idle. If they detect an idle medium, they begin transmitting. If two or more devices transmit at the same time, a collision occurs. Immediately after a collision occurs, the two stations involved stop transmitting. After that, they send out a jam signal. Then, the two stations back off for a random interval, and the transmission process begins again.
whyWrong: The random backoff interval comes after the jam signal, not immediately after the collision.
The jam signal is sent after the stations have stopped transmitting their frames.
Listening for an idle channel happens before transmitting and again after the backoff, not right after the collision.
Retransmission is the last step, after the jam signal and the backoff interval.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 47
note: CSMA/CD is not named in N10-009; tagged to Layer 2 (Data link) as the closest topic.

stem: For the Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD) mechanism to function properly on an Ethernet network, host systems must be able to detect when a collision occurs so they can react to it. Which of the following cabling errors can prevent the collision detection process from functioning properly?
options: Too many systems on a single network
explanation: For CSMA/CD to function properly, a system must detect a packet collision while it is transmitting the packet. If cable segments are too long, the packet might leave the transmitting system before the collision is detected, resulting in a late collision, which cannot be retransmitted. Incorrect pinouts, too many systems, and excessive collisions typically will not prevent the collision detection system from occurring.
whyWrong: Incorrect pinouts cause connection or signal faults but do not stop the collision detection process itself.
Too many systems cause more collisions, but the stations can still detect them.
Many collisions slow the network, but each one can still be detected and retransmitted.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 48
note: CSMA/CD is not named in N10-009; tagged to Layer 2 (Data link) as the closest topic.

stem: When a packet collision between two systems occurs on an Ethernet network, Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD) causes the two systems to stop transmitting and generate a jam signal. After sending the jam signal, why do the two systems wait for a randomized backoff interval before retransmitting their packets?
options: They need time to reassemble the packets.
To prevent another collision from occurring.
They need to rebuffer the packet.
To recalculate the packets' checksum values.
explanation: After transmitting their jam signals, the two systems wait for a randomized interval. This is to prevent them from retransmitting their packets at the same time, resulting in another collision. It is not necessary for the systems to reassemble, rebuffer, or recalculate checksums for their packets.
whyWrong: The frames are not broken up by a collision, so the stations do not need time to reassemble them.
The stations still hold the frame in their buffers, so no rebuffering is needed.
The frame content does not change, so the checksum does not have to be recalculated.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 49
note: CSMA/CD is not named in N10-009; tagged to Layer 2 (Data link) as the closest topic.

stem: Which of the following statements is true about an Ethernet network that uses CSMA/CD?
options: Collisions never occur unless there is a network fault.
Collisions cause data to be irretrievably lost.
Collisions are the result of duplicate IP addresses.
explanation: Collisions are a normal occurrence on an Ethernet network; they occur when two nodes transmit at exactly the same time. There need not be a network fault for collisions to occur. When collisions occur, the nodes involved retransmit their packets so that no data is lost. Collisions are a phenomenon of Data link layer protocols; they have nothing to do with IP addresses, which are Network layer constructs.
whyWrong: Collisions happen whenever two stations transmit at once, even when nothing is faulty.
CSMA/CD retransmits the frames after a collision, so no data is lost.
Duplicate IP addresses are a Network layer problem and do not cause Ethernet collisions.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 51
note: CSMA/CD is not named in N10-009; tagged to Layer 2 (Data link) as the closest topic.

stem: Which of the following is an abnormal occurrence on an Ethernet network?
explanation: Collisions are a normal occurrence on an Ethernet network, but late collisions are not normal. Late collisions occur when two packets collide after one or more finishes transmitting. Packet retransmissions, collision detection, and jam signals are all normal occurrences on an Ethernet network.
whyWrong: Retransmitting frames after a collision is a normal part of CSMA/CD.
Detecting collisions is the normal job of CSMA/CD on a shared Ethernet segment.
A jam signal is the normal response that stations send after they detect a collision.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 52
note: CSMA/CD is not named in N10-009; tagged to Layer 2 (Data link) as the closest topic.

stem: A switch with auto-medium-dependent interface crossover (MDI-X) ports eliminates the need for which of the following?
explanation: Ethernet implementations, such as 100Base-TX, which use separate wire pairs for transmitting and receiving data, require a crossover circuit to ensure that the transmit pins on each end of a connection are wired to the receive pins at the other end. This crossover circuit can be implemented in a patch cable—called a crossover cable—or by a switch port. Switches with auto-medium-dependent interface crossover (MDI-X) ports can detect the need for a crossover circuit and implement it automatically in the port. This eliminates the need for crossover cables. Auto-medium-dependent interface crossover (MDI-X) ports do not eliminate the need for 8P8C connectors, connections between switches, or straight-through cables.
whyWrong: Twisted-pair Ethernet ports still need 8P8C (RJ45) connectors.
Switches must still be connected to each other to expand the network.
Straight-through cables are still needed and are the normal cable for these connections.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 61
note: MDI/MDI-X and crossover cables are not named in N10-009; tagged to wired media (802.3 standards).

stem: Which of the following cable types is needed to connect an MDI port on a workstation to an MDI-X port on an Ethernet switch?
explanation: When connecting an MDI port to an MDI-X port, the necessary crossover circuit is implemented in the MDI-X port. Therefore, the connection needs a straight-through cable and there is no need for a crossover cable. MDI and MDI-X ports are used only with twisted-pair cables, so there is no need for coaxial or fiber-optic cables.
whyWrong: A crossover cable would add a second crossover to the one in the MDI-X port, so transmit would meet transmit.
MDI and MDI-X ports are twisted-pair ports, so coaxial cable cannot connect to them.
Single-mode fiber needs fiber ports and transceivers, not MDI or MDI-X twisted-pair ports.
Multimode fiber needs fiber ports and transceivers, not MDI or MDI-X twisted-pair ports.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 62
note: MDI/MDI-X and crossover cables are not named in N10-009; tagged to wired media (802.3 standards).

stem: Which of the following identifiers does a switch use to forward incoming packets out through the correct ports?
explanation: Switches use media access control (MAC) addresses to identify the ports associated with specific hosts. The switch reads the destination MAC address from each incoming packet and forwards it out through the port associated with that address. Switches are Data link layer devices, so they do not use IP addresses or DNS names to forward packets. The maximum transmission unit (MTU) value specifies the maximum size of Data link layer frames; the switch does not use it to forward packets.
whyWrong: IP addresses are Network layer addresses that routers use, not switches.
DNS names are resolved by DNS servers and are not used to forward frames.
The MTU sets the largest frame size and is not used to choose an outgoing port.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 64

stem: Ralph has been hired by a company to redesign its local area network (LAN). Right now, it has a single 100 Mbps Ethernet LAN with 40 users and two shared servers, all connected through three hubs. The users on the network must be able to share files with one another and also access the shared servers. The users are complaining that the network is too slow. Management states that cost is a factor that must be considered. Which of the following upgrade scenarios should Ralph recommend in this situation?
options: Split the network into smaller segments with dedicated hubs as opposed to shared hubs.
Split the network into two routed LANs with 20 users each.
Replace the hubs with switches to define separate collision domains and filter unnecessary traffic from each segment.
Replace the hubs with a layer 3 switch and define two virtual LANs (VLANs) with 20 users each.
explanation: The best choice is to replace the hubs with switches, since the network is relatively small and cost is an issue. On the existing network, all users share the same 100 Mbps communication channel, and each computer must take turns transmitting. By replacing the hubs with switches, you provide each computer with a dedicated 100 Mbps connection to the switch, while reducing unnecessary traffic and collisions on the network. There is no such thing as a dedicated hub. Splitting the network into two routed LANs is not the best solution, because all users must share information on a constant basis. Also, cost is a factor, and routers are more expensive than switches. Replacing the hubs with a layer 3 switch and defining two VLANs with 20 users each is not a reasonable solution because layer 3 switches are very expensive.
whyWrong: Dedicated hubs do not exist, and any hub still shares one collision domain among its ports.
Splitting into routed LANs costs more and gets in the way of users who constantly share files with each other.
A layer 3 switch with VLANs is expensive and adds routing between users who must share files constantly.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 66

stem: A multilayer switch typically functions at which layers of the OSI reference model? (Choose two.)
explanation: All switches operate at the Data link layer of the OSI model, but multilayer switches usually also function as routers, which are Network layer devices, through the use of a switch virtual interface (SVI). They are not usually transport or Application layer devices.
whyWrong: Multilayer switches do not usually work at the Transport layer.
Multilayer switches do not usually work at the Application layer, which content switches do.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 68

stem: A small business office currently has a 1000Base-T Ethernet network with a single eight-port switch. All of the switchports are populated, and the business owner wants to expand the network further. However, the switch does not have an uplink port. The owner has purchased a new switch, also with eight ports, that does have an uplink port, but he does not know how to connect them together. What must the owner do to install the new switch on the network?
options: Use a standard patch cable to connect a standard port on the existing switch to a standard port on the new switch.
Use a standard patch cable to connect a standard port on the existing switch to the uplink port on the new switch.
Purchase a crossover cable and use it to connect a standard port on the existing switch to the uplink port on the new switch.
Purchase a second new switch with an uplink port to replace the old one and use a standard patch cable to connect the two uplink ports together.
explanation: Standard switchports have a crossover circuit, which ensures that the transmit signals at one end of the connection arrive at the receive pins at the other end. The uplink port in a switch bypasses the crossover circuit, so that two connected switches do not have crossover circuits that cancel each other out. A connection between a standard port and an uplink port, using a standard cable, results in a single crossover, which is correct wiring. Each of the other solutions results in either two crossovers or no crossovers, both of which are incorrect.
whyWrong: Two standard ports each have a crossover circuit, so a standard cable between them gives two crossovers that cancel out.
A crossover cable to the uplink port adds a crossover to the one in the standard port, so the wiring is crossed twice.
A standard cable between two uplink ports gives no crossover at all, so transmit meets transmit.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 70
note: The book's correct option says 'uplink port on the new hub'; changed to 'new switch' to match the stem. Most current 1000Base-T switches use Auto-MDI-X, so uplink ports are rarely needed today. MDI/MDI-X and crossover cables are not named in N10-009; tagged to wired media.

stem: Which of the following mechanisms for load balancing web servers is able to read the incoming HTTP and HTTPS requests and perform advanced functions based on the information they contain?
explanation: A content switch is an Application layer device, which is what renders it capable of reading the incoming Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) and Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) messages. HTTP is an Application layer protocol. Multilayer switches do not operate above the Transport layer. Failover clustering and (DNS) round-robin are both techniques for distributing incoming traffic without actually processing it.
whyWrong: Multilayer switches do not work above the Transport layer, so they cannot read HTTP requests.
Failover clustering moves work to another server when one fails and does not read the requests.
Round-robin DNS hands out server addresses in turn without reading the HTTP requests.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 78

stem: Which of the following bridging types has never been used on Ethernet local area networks (LANs)?
explanation: Source route bridging was a technique used on token ring (and not Ethernet) networks, in which a routing information field (RIF) in the packet header identified the network segments the packet should follow to reach its destination. Store and forward, transparent, and multiport bridges have all been used on Ethernet networks.
whyWrong: Store-and-forward bridges, which receive a whole frame before forwarding it, have been used on Ethernet.
Transparent bridges, which learn MAC addresses on their own, are the normal Ethernet bridge type.
Multiport bridges, which are the basis of Ethernet switches, have been used on Ethernet.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 80
note: Bridging types are not named in N10-009; tagged to Layer 2 (Data link) as the closest topic.

stem: Which of the following IEEE standards calls for the use of the Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance (CSMA/CA) Media Access Control (MAC) mechanism?
explanation: The IEEE 802.11ac standard, like all of the wireless LAN standards in the 802.11 working group, uses CSMA/CA for MAC. The 802.1X standard defines an authentication mechanism and does not require a MAC mechanism. The IEEE 802.3 (Ethernet) standard uses Carrier-Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD).
whyWrong: IEEE 802.1X is an authentication standard and does not define a media access method.
IEEE 802.3 Ethernet uses CSMA/CD, not CSMA/CA.
Only the 802.11 wireless standard uses CSMA/CA, so not all of the listed standards do.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 84

stem: Which of the following wireless networking technologies will never experience interference from a 2.4 GHz wireless phone? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: IEEE 802.11b, 802.11g, 802.11n, and 802.11ax networks can use the 2.4 GHz frequency band for their transmissions, which can experience interference from a wireless phone using the same frequency. IEEE 802.11a and IEEE 802.11ac, however, use the 5 GHz band, which will not experience interference from a 2.4 GHz phone.
whyWrong: IEEE 802.11b uses only the 2.4 GHz band, so a 2.4 GHz phone can interfere with it.
IEEE 802.11g uses only the 2.4 GHz band, so a 2.4 GHz phone can interfere with it.
IEEE 802.11n can use the 2.4 GHz band, so a 2.4 GHz phone can interfere with it.
IEEE 802.11ax can use the 2.4 GHz band, so a 2.4 GHz phone can interfere with it.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 87

stem: Which of the following wireless LAN standards include the ability to use multiple input, multiple output (MIMO) antennas? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: The IEEE 802.11n, 802.11ac, and 802.11ax standards include MIMO, which enables them to effectively multiplex signals using multiple antennas. This capability was first introduced in the 802.11n standard, so the 802.11a and 802.11b/g standards do not support it.
whyWrong: IEEE 802.11a uses a single antenna stream and came before MIMO was introduced.
IEEE 802.11b and 802.11g came before MIMO, which was first introduced in 802.11n.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 88

stem: Which of the following IEEE wireless LAN standards uses the direct-sequence spread spectrum (DSSS) signal modulation technique?
explanation: The IEEE 802.11b standard calls for DSSS signal modulation. All of the other standards listed call for orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) encoding.
whyWrong: IEEE 802.11a uses OFDM, not DSSS.
IEEE 802.11g uses OFDM for its higher speeds, not DSSS.
IEEE 802.11n uses OFDM with MIMO, not DSSS.
IEEE 802.11ac uses OFDM with MU-MIMO, not DSSS.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 89

stem: How do wireless networking devices conforming to the IEEE 802.11n and 802.11ac standards achieve transmission speeds greater than 72.2 Mbps?
options: By using direct-sequence spread spectrum (DSSS) modulation
By using multiple antennas to transmit several data streams simultaneously
By using frequencies in the 5 GHz band
By sacrificing transmission range for speed
explanation: The IEEE 802.11n and 802.11ac standards support a transmission technique called multiple input, multiple output (MIMO), which combines the bandwidth of multiple data streams to achieve greater throughput. IEEE 802.11n and 802.11ac do use the 5 GHz band, but this in itself does not yield greater transmission speeds. The specified standards do not call for the use of DSSS modulation, nor do they sacrifice range for speed. In fact, 802.11n and 802.11ac networks can achieve greater ranges than the previous technologies.
whyWrong: IEEE 802.11n and 802.11ac use OFDM, not DSSS, which is the older 802.11b method.
Using the 5 GHz band does not by itself raise the speed above 72.2 Mbps.
These standards do not give up range for speed and can reach farther than older standards.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 91

stem: What is the term for the technology implemented in the IEEE 802.11ac standard that enables a wireless device to transmit multiple frames to multiple clients simultaneously?
explanation: The multiple input, multiple output (MIMO) technology introduced in the IEEE 802.11n standard enables wireless devices to transmit and receive signals using multiple antennas simultaneously. The multiuser MIMO (MU-MIMO) variant defined in the 802.11ac standard advances this technique by enabling wireless devices to transmit multiple frames to different users simultaneously, using multiple antennas. Carrier-Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance (CSMA/CA) is a Media Access Control (MAC) mechanism used by all 802.11 networks. Channel bonding is a wireless networking technique that combines channels to increase bandwidth.
whyWrong: MIMO uses multiple antennas for one client at a time, not multiple clients at once.
Channel bonding combines channels for more bandwidth but does not send to several clients at once.
CSMA/CA is the media access method of all 802.11 networks, not a way to send to several clients at once.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 94

stem: Which of the following terms defines a wireless LAN transmission technique in which devices use multiple antennas to increase transmission speeds?
explanation: Multiple input, multiple output (MIMO) calls for the use of two or more antennas, enabling wireless devices to effectively multiplex signals, thereby increasing their transmission speeds. Time-division multiple access (TDMA) is a communication technique that splits a frequency into multiple time slots, enabling it to carry multiple data streams. A personal area network (PAN) provides communication among devices associated with a single person, such as smartphones. Ant+ is a wireless protocol that is typically used to monitor data gathered by sensors, such as those in cardiac pacemakers.
whyWrong: TDMA splits one frequency into time slots for several data streams and does not use multiple antennas.
A PAN is a small network around one person, not a transmission technique.
ANT+ is a low-power wireless protocol for sensors, not a multi-antenna technique.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 96

stem: Which of the following wireless networking standards are capable of using only the 5 GHz frequency? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: The IEEE 802.11a and IEEE 802.11ac standards can use the 5 GHz band only. IEEE 802.11b and IEEE 802.11g can use the 2.4 GHz band only. IEEE 802.11n and IEEE 802.11ax can use either the 2.4 or the 5 GHz band.
whyWrong: IEEE 802.11b uses only the 2.4 GHz band.
IEEE 802.11g uses only the 2.4 GHz band.
IEEE 802.11n can use both the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.
IEEE 802.11ax can use the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz bands.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 98

stem: Which of the following IEEE wireless LAN standards provides the greatest possible throughput?
explanation: The IEEE 802.11ax standard provides the greatest possible throughput, up to a theoretical maximum of 9.6 Gbps. This is a 37% improvement over 802.11ac, at 7 Gbps. The 802.11n standard runs at speeds up to 600 Mbps. The 802.11a and 802.11g standards run at up to 54 Mbps. The 802.11b standard runs at up to 11 Mbps.
whyWrong: IEEE 802.11a runs at up to 54 Mbps.
IEEE 802.11ac reaches about 7 Gbps, which is less than 802.11ax.
IEEE 802.11b runs at up to 11 Mbps.
IEEE 802.11g runs at up to 54 Mbps.
IEEE 802.11n runs at up to 600 Mbps.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 100

stem: Which of the following IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN standards are capable of supporting both the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz frequencies? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: The 802.11n and 802.11ax standards define wireless LAN devices that can support both the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz frequency bands. The 802.11a and 802.11ac standards use only 5 GHz, and the 802.11b and 802.11g standards use only 2.4 GHz.
whyWrong: IEEE 802.11a uses only the 5 GHz band.
IEEE 802.11b uses only the 2.4 GHz band.
IEEE 802.11g uses only the 2.4 GHz band.
IEEE 802.11ac uses only the 5 GHz band.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 101

stem: What is the maximum number of transmit and receive antennas supported by the currently ratified IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN standards?
explanation: The 802.11ax and 802.11ac standards support multiple input, multiple output (MIMO) through the use of up to eight antennas on a single device. 802.11n is the only earlier 802.11 standard that supports MIMO, but it can only use a maximum of four antennas.
whyWrong: Two antennas is far below the MIMO limit of 802.11n and later standards.
Four antennas is the limit of 802.11n, while 802.11ac and 802.11ax support more.
Sixteen antennas is more than 802.11ac and 802.11ax support.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 102
note: Book answer reflects 802.11ac/ax; the newer IEEE 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7) standard defines up to 16 spatial streams.

stem: At which layer of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model do wireless range extenders operate?
explanation: Wireless range extenders are Physical layer devices that receive signals from wireless access points (WAPs) and network adapters and retransmit them, enabling devices to connect that are farther apart than the network would normally support. Because the extenders do not process the packets in any way, but just retransmit the signals, they do not operate at any layer above the Physical.
whyWrong: Range extenders retransmit signals without reading the frame addresses, so the book places them below the Data link layer.
Range extenders do not route packets, so they do not work at the Network layer.
Range extenders do not manage segments or connections, so they do not work at the Transport layer.
Range extenders do not manage sessions, so they do not work at the Session layer.
Range extenders do not convert or encrypt data formats, so they do not work at the Presentation layer.
Range extenders do not provide user services, so they do not work at the Application layer.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 105
note: Book answer is debatable: many wireless range extenders (repeaters) associate with the AP and forward 802.11 frames, which some sources place at Layer 2.

stem: Which of the following is the maximum theoretical download speed for a 5G cellular network?
explanation: The 5G cellular network specification calls for maximum theoretical download speeds of 10 Gbps, although the actual speed realized will be less. Actual 5G speeds depend on the frequency band in use, the distance to the tower, and the number of users sharing the cell. The high-band frequencies give the fastest speeds but have a short range.
whyWrong: 42 Mbps is a typical 3G HSPA+ figure, far below the 5G specification.
150 Mbps is in the range of 4G LTE, not the 5G maximum.
1 Gbps is the 4G LTE-Advanced target, not the 5G theoretical maximum.
100 Gbps is far above the 5G specification's theoretical maximum.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 128

stem: Which of the following statements about 5G cellular networks are true? (Choose all that apply.)
options: 5G networks can operate on three frequency bands.
5G networks with the highest speeds also have a more limited range.
4G devices can connect to 5G networks at reduced speeds.
On a 5G network, the lower frequency bands provide the highest speeds.
explanation: 5G networks can operate on three frequency bands—low, medium, and high—with the high frequencies having the fastest speeds and reduced range. 4G devices cannot function on 5G networks.
whyWrong: 4G devices cannot use 5G networks, because 5G uses a different radio interface.
On 5G, the high frequency bands give the highest speeds, while the low bands give the longest range.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 2: Network Implementation, Review Questions question 129

stem: Alice has been hired by a corporation to design the cabling for their network. The corporation just moved into two different floors of an older building: a retail space on the ground floor and an office space on the 43rd floor. The building has existing Category 5e (CAT 5e) unshielded twisted-pair (UTP) cable. Alice's client wants two separate local area networks (LANs), one on each of the two floors, with a backbone network connecting them. They want a 1 gigabit-per-second (Gbps) data rate for each LAN but plan on migrating to 10 Gbps in the future. The two networks are approximately 200 meters apart. Which of the following solutions BEST meets the client's needs?
options: Install Category 6 (CAT 6) or Category 6a (CAT 6a) UTP cable for the LANs. These cables run at 1 Gbps and provide a migration path to 10 Gbps. Use twisted-pair cable for the backbone network.
Use the existing CAT 5e cabling for the LANs, since CAT 5e runs at 1 Gbps. Use thick coaxial cable for the backbone network.
Install CAT 6 or CAT 6a UTP cable for the LANs. These cables run at 1 Gbps and provide a migration path to 10 Gbps. Use multimode fiber-optic cable for the backbone network.
Install CAT 6 or CAT 6a UTP cable for the LANs. These cables run at 1 Gbps and provide a migration path to 10 Gbps. Use the existing CAT 5e cable for the backbone network.
Replace the UTP cables with shielded twisted-pair (STP) cables.
explanation: Either CAT 6 or CAT 6a UTP cable will provide the currently required 1 Gbps data rate, with a migration path to 10 Gbps in the future. The backbone cabling connecting the two LANs needs to be fiber-optic, since it exceeds the distance limitations of twisted-pair and coaxial cable. CAT 5e cable conceivably runs at 1 Gbps; however, it does not run at 10 Gbps. Shielded cable alone would not guarantee a 1 Gbps data rate and an upgrade path to 10 Gbps.
whyWrong: Twisted-pair segments are limited to 100 meters, too short for a 200-meter backbone.
CAT 5e cannot carry 10 Gbps, and thick coaxial cable is an obsolete backbone medium that cannot meet the future speed.
CAT 5e twisted pair cannot span 200 meters and does not provide the 10 Gbps upgrade path.
Shielding alone does not raise the data rate to 10 Gbps or extend the 100-meter twisted-pair limit for the backbone.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 5: Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 76

stem: A maintenance worker, while replacing a light fixture in an office building, accidentally severs a network cable in the drop ceiling. The tenants use a variety of local area network (LAN) technologies throughout the structure, but on that particular floor, there are three separate LANs: a 10-node Thin Ethernet LAN using coaxial cable in a bus topology, a 25-node Gigabit Ethernet LAN using twisted-pair cable in a star/hub and spoke topology, and a 5-node Fiber Distributed Data Interface (FDDI) LAN using multimode fiber-optic cable in a double ring topology. Without knowing which of the LANs the severed cable belongs to, what is the maximum number of computers that could be directly affected by the cable break?
explanation: The Thin Ethernet LAN is the network most endangered by the cable break. If a bus network is severed, all of the workstations on it are affected because the cable segments are no longer terminated at one end. The Gigabit Ethernet network uses a star/hub and spoke topology, which means that only the one computer using the severed cable could be disconnected from the network. An FDDI double ring network can survive a single cable break without any workstations being affected.
whyWrong: A break in the bus network cable removes the termination and stops every node on that segment.
One computer is the worst case for the star network, but the bus network loses all of its nodes.
The five FDDI nodes are protected by the double ring, which survives a single break.
In the star network, a cut cable disconnects only the one computer that uses it.
The three networks are separate, so one severed cable cannot affect all 40 computers.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 5: Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 77

stem: Which of the following twisted-pair cable types can you use to construct a 10GBase-T network with 100-meter segments? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: Category 6a (CAT 6a) twisted-pair cable is a variant on CAT 6 that enables you to create 10GBase-T networks with segments up to 100 meters long. Category 7 (CAT 7) cable adds shielding both to the individual wire pairs and to the entire cable, for even greater resistance to crosstalk and noise. CAT 7 supports 100-meter 10GBase-T segments as well. CAT 8 cable supports bandwidth up to 2 GHz, making it even more suitable for 10GBase-T networks than CAT 6a (500 MHz) or CAT7 (600 MHz). CAT 5 and CAT 5e are not suitable for use with 10GBase-T. You can use CAT 6 for 10Gbase-T, but it is limited to 55-meter segments.
whyWrong: CAT 5 is rated for 100 Mbps and cannot carry 10GBase-T.
CAT 5e is rated for 1 Gbps and cannot carry 10GBase-T.
CAT 6 carries 10GBase-T only on segments up to about 55 meters.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 5: Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 78

stem: Which of the following twisted-pair cable types are rated for 1,000 megabit-per-second (Mbps) Gigabit Ethernet using two wire pairs? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: All twisted-pair Gigabit Ethernet implementations require all four wire pairs to achieve 1,000 Mbps transfer rates. 10Base-T and 100Base-TX use only two of the four wire pairs, but 1000Base-T transmits on all four pairs at the same time. Therefore no cable category can run 1000 Mbps Ethernet on two pairs.
whyWrong: CAT 5 cannot run Gigabit Ethernet on two pairs, because 1000Base-T needs all four pairs.
CAT 5e supports 1000Base-T only when all four pairs are used.
CAT 6 supports Gigabit Ethernet only when all four pairs are used.
CAT 6a supports Gigabit Ethernet only when all four pairs are used.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 5: Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 79

stem: Which of the following twisted-pair cable types support both 10-megabit-per-second (Mbps) and 100 Mbps data rates, using only two pairs? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: CAT 5 cable was the original cable standard intended for transfer rates up to 100 Mbps. CAT 5e, CAT 6, and CAT 6a all support 100 Mbps and are also rated for data rates up to 1,000 Mbps. CAT 6 and CAT 6a can also support 10 Gbps. All of these standards also support the 10 Mbps transfer rate.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 5: Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 80

stem: Ed has been hired to install network cabling for a small private company with 15 employees who need to share files and printers. All of the employees are physically located within the same building in two separate office spaces directly adjacent to each other, sharing a common wall and door for access. Both offices have drop ceilings. The client wants a simple Gigabit Ethernet installation that is easy to troubleshoot. In addition, Ed's client wants to keep installation costs to a minimum. Which of the following combinations of topology, cable type, and installation method would BEST meet the needs of Ed's client?
options: Star/hub and spoke topology, fiber-optic cabling, and internal installation
Bus topology, coaxial cabling, and external installation
Bus topology, twisted-pair cabling, and internal installation
Star/hub and spoke topology, coaxial cabling, and external installation
Star/hub and spoke topology, twisted-pair cabling, and external installation
explanation: Because the company has few employees, a single location, and cost restrictions, the best solution is a star/hub and spoke topology with prefabricated twisted-pair cabling and an external installation method. The star/hub and spoke topology uses a central switch. Prefabricated twisted-pair cabling, with the connectors already attached, will keep the cost to a minimum. Since the employees are all located in the same building, with a common wall and a drop ceiling, the external installation method is the best choice. It is not possible to use a bus topology or coaxial cable for Gigabit Ethernet. Ed could use fiber-optic cable in a star/hub and spoke topology for Gigabit Ethernet, but it is more difficult and expensive to install. An internal installation, which uses a combination of bulk cable and prefabricated cables, is more expensive than an external installation and is typically used for larger networks.
whyWrong: Fiber-optic cable and an internal installation would work but cost far more than the client wants to spend.
A bus topology on coaxial cable cannot carry Gigabit Ethernet.
Gigabit Ethernet does not use a bus topology, and an internal installation adds cost.
Coaxial cable cannot carry Gigabit Ethernet, even in a star topology.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 5: Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 81

stem: Ed has been hired by a company to upgrade its network infrastructure. The current network is 10 Mbps Ethernet running on Category 5 (CAT 5) twisted-pair cable. There are 100 computers on the network, all of which have 10/100/1000 multispeed network interface adapters. The computers are all connected to hubs. Users are complaining that the network is too slow, and connections are sometimes dropped. Management wants to upgrade to the fastest Ethernet standard possible using the existing cabling, and still keep costs to a minimum. Which of the following implementations should Ed recommend to the client?
options: Upgrade to 100Base-TX and keep the existing hubs.
Upgrade to 1000Base-T and keep the existing hubs.
Upgrade to 100Base-FX and replace all of the hubs with switches.
Upgrade to 1000Base-T and replace all of the hubs with switches.
Upgrade to 100Base-SX and replace all of the hubs with switches.
explanation: The best solution in this scenario is to upgrade to 1000Base-T and replace the existing hubs with switches. 1000Base-T provides the fastest transfer speeds supported by the existing cable. Since users are complaining that the network is slow with the existing hubs, it makes sense to replace the shared hub environment with switches that offer dedicated bandwidth on each port. Any solution that does not replace the hubs would not address the users' complaints. 100Base-TX would provide a speed increase, but it runs at ~1/10 the speed of 1000Base-TX. Upgrading to 100Base-FX or 100Base-SX would require the cabling to be replaced with fiber-optic, which would be very expensive.
whyWrong: Keeping the hubs leaves a shared collision domain, so the slowdowns and dropped connections continue.
Keeping the hubs leaves shared bandwidth and collisions, so the users' complaints are not solved.
100Base-FX needs fiber-optic cable, which would mean replacing all of the existing cabling.
100Base-SX runs on fiber-optic cable, which would mean replacing all of the existing cabling.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 5: Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 82

stem: Ralph has been asked to create some new patch cables that will be used to connect patch panel ports to the network switches. He has been told to use the T568B pinout standard for all of the cable connectors. Ralph gathers the materials and the tools needed to complete the task, but he is not sure about the T568B pinout. Which of the following pinouts must Ralph use when creating the patch cables?
options: White/orange, orange, white/green, blue, white/blue, green, white/brown, brown
White/green, green, white/orange, blue, white/blue, orange, white/brown, brown
White/orange, orange, white/green, green, white/blue, blue, white/brown, brown
White/brown, white/green, white/orange, blue, white/blue, orange, green, brown
explanation: The T568B pinout, in order from pin 1 to pin 8, is white/orange, orange, white/green, blue, white/blue, green, white/brown, brown. This is the sequence Ralph must use when he attaches the connectors. The T568A pinout swaps the orange and green pairs, so it would also work, but Ralph has been told not to use it. The other sequences do not keep each twisted pair on the correct pins and can result in excessive crosstalk.
whyWrong: This sequence is the T568A pinout, which Ralph was told not to use.
This sequence splits the blue and green pairs incorrectly and can cause excessive crosstalk.
This sequence matches neither T568A nor T568B and would leave the pairs split.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 5: Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 83

stem: Which of the following devices can you use to connect two multimode fiber-optic Ethernet networks in different buildings 2,000 meters apart using a single-mode fiber-optic cable segment running at the same speed, while maintaining a single collision domain?
explanation: A media converter is a Physical layer device that can connect different types of network media together, as long as they have the same speed and duplex settings. Because the converter simply retransmits the signals, the single-collision domain is maintained. Bridges and switches are Data link layer devices that create multiple-collision domains. Routers are Network layer devices that create separate collision and broadcast domains.
whyWrong: A bridge is a Data Link layer device that splits the network into separate collision domains.
A switch is a Data Link layer device that gives each port its own collision domain.
A router is a Network layer device that creates separate collision and broadcast domains.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 5: Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 85
note: Media converters are not named in N10-009; tagged with the transceivers topic.

stem: Which of the following IP address assignments indicates that a computer has been unable to communicate with a DHCP server?
explanation: The address 169.254.199.22 is from the 169.254.0.0/16 network address assigned to Automatic Private IP Addressing (APIPA), a standard for the assignment of IP addresses to Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) clients when they cannot obtain an address from a DHCP server. 127.0.0.1 is the standard IPv4 loopback address. 240.15.167.251 is from the 240.0.0.0 network address, which is reserved for experimental use. Neither of these are ever assigned by DHCP. 255.255.255.0 is not an IP address at all; it is a subnet mask.
whyWrong: 127.0.0.1 is the IPv4 loopback address, which DHCP never assigns.
255.255.255.0 is a subnet mask, not an IP address.
240.15.167.251 is in the reserved Class E range, which DHCP never assigns.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 5: Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 96

stem: Which of the following Application layer protocols includes a program that enables a user to log on to a network device and execute commands on the remote system using a command-line interface? (Choose all that apply.)
explanation: Both Telnet and FTP are protocols that include command-line client applications, with Telnet providing terminal emulation and FTP file transfer functionality. SNMP and DNS are both Application layer protocols, but neither one includes a program. Nslookup has a command-line interface, but it executes commands on the local system, not a remote one.
whyWrong: SNMP manages and monitors devices and does not provide a remote command-line logon.
DNS resolves names and does not include a remote command-line client.
`nslookup` runs commands on the local system and is a tool, not an Application layer protocol.
source: CompTIA Network+ Practice Tests: Exam N10-009 (Zacker) – Chapter 5: Network Troubleshooting, Review Questions question 230
note: Book answer is debatable: FTP is a file transfer client, not a remote command-execution program. Telnet/FTP are in the 1.4 protocols table.
